newsitem.title: UK: N. Irish politician Hume may seek Irish presidency.
newsitem.headline: N. Irish politician Hume may seek Irish presidency.

text.p: John Hume, a moderate Irish nationalist and an architect of the Northern Ireland peace process, may not seek reelection to the British parliament in the coming general election, a colleague said on Friday.
Speculation is growing in the Republic of Ireland that Hume could seek the Irish presidency if current head of state Mary Robinson decides not to seek a second term.
Under the Irish constitution, anyone in the British province of Northern Ireland has the right to be regarded as an Irish citizen and therefore to stand for the presidency.
Joe Hendron, a member of the British parliament for Hume's Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), told Irish radio Hume had discussed options with the party but had not yet made a decision.
"He has the massive role, not only of leader of the SDLP, but also as a member of the European Parliament. He has not made up his mind yet as to whether he will run," Hendron said.
The next British parliamentary election must be held by May this year. Hume declined to say in a radio interview on Thursday whether he would stand in his Foyle constituency in Londonderry.
Robinson is due to announce in the next few weeks whether she will seek a second term in November. If she does, she is likely to be unopposed -- Hume would not stand against her.
Similarly, Hume is unlikely to be opposed by anyone from the main Irish political parties if his name goes forward.
Britain's Guardian newspaper said Robinson had lent weight to the previously symbolic role of the president.
"As a consequence, the suitability of the position as a vehicle for promoting the peace process might appeal to Mr Hume, whose popularity with Irish voters is constant," it said.

Hume has been a prime mover in the drive to find a political solution to the conflict in Northern Ireland. Irish Republican Army guerrillas, fighting against British rule of the province, ended a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996.

The Guardian said there concerns within the SDLP that Hume's seat could fall to Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, if Hume, with his large personal support, did not stand. That would boost Sinn Fein's efforts to become the main Irish nationalist party in Northern Ireland.
